readingInstruction: Read 2 Corinthians 10:1-13:14. Paul’s tone shifts here, as he defends his apostleship against false teachers. Read with an ear for his irony and his pain. Pay special attention to the thorn in the flesh and the answer he received in 12:7-10.
settingTheScene: Some in Corinth, influenced by self-styled “super-apostles,” dismissed Paul as unimpressive in person and contemptible in speech. They boasted of credentials, visions, and eloquence. Paul is reluctant to boast, but to defend the gospel he does a kind of “fool’s boasting” in which he boasts of his weaknesses. This section reverses worldly values and gives one of the Bible’s most important teachings on God’s strength in weakness.
observation: “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds” (10:4).
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (10:17).
“But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ” (11:3).
“If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (11:30).
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
“For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10).
“Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves” (13:5).
“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (13:14).
interpretation:
Paul begins by appealing “by the meekness and gentleness of Christ.” He is accused of being bold when away and timid when present. He warns that when he comes, he may have to be bold. “For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds. We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ.” The spiritual battle is fought with truth, prayer, and the word, not with manipulation or force. He refuses to compare himself with those who commend themselves. “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.”

In chapter 11, Paul’s jealousy for the church leads him to a painful comparison. He has betrothed them to one husband, to present them as a pure virgin to Christ. “But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.” The false teachers preach another Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. Paul calls them “false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.” Their credentials are impressive, but Paul tallies his own: far more labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, often near death. Five times he received thirty-nine lashes; three times beaten with rods; once stoned; three times shipwrecked; a night and a day adrift at sea; in danger from rivers, robbers, his own people, Gentiles, the city, the wilderness, false brothers; in toil and hardship, sleepless nights, hunger, cold. “And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.” Then: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness,” and he tells of being lowered in a basket through a window in the wall at Damascus.

In chapter 12, he speaks of a vision, “a man in Christ” caught up to the third heaven, hearing things that cannot be told. He refrains from boasting of this. “So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me.” We do not know what the thorn was: an illness, a person, a temptation. Three times he pleaded with the Lord to remove it. “But he said to me, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me. For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” God’s answer was not removal but sufficiency. This verse has comforted countless suffering believers.

Paul closes with warnings and tenderness. He fears he will find quarreling, jealousy, and unrepentance. “Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?” The aim is restoration, not demolition. “Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.” The letter ends with the benediction: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” It is one of the clearest Trinitarian blessings in the New Testament.
connection: Jeremiah 9:23-24 is the source of 10:17. Genesis 3 describes the serpent’s deceit. Galatians 1:6-9 also warns of false gospels. Ephesians 6:10-18 describes spiritual warfare. Acts 9:23-25 and 14:19 tell of the basket and the stoning. Job 1 to 2 shows Satan allowed to afflict. Isaiah 40:28-31 promises strength to the weary. Philippians 4:13 says I can do all things through him who strengthens me. Hebrews 4:15-16 offers grace to help in time of need. Romans 8:35-39 and 1 Peter 5:10 speak of suffering and grace.
application:
Name your “thorn.” Bring it to the Lord as Paul did. Listen for his answer.

Read 12:9 aloud and apply it to a current weakness.

Examine yourself as 13:5 says. Is Christ in you? Do you have the marks of faith?
prayerPrompts: Bring God your “thorn,” and tell him what it is.
Thank him that his grace is sufficient and his power is perfected in weakness.
Ask him to teach you to boast in weakness.
